source.title: From Rage to Refusal: Using Social-Media Data to Steer Partisan Affect in LLMs
source.citation: From Rage to Refusal: Using Social-Me…

page_placements.theme: Off-target steering induces refusal (refusal as a fallback state)

record.tranche_reason: The study compares hostility directions with measured refusal directions and orthogonalizes hostility vectors against refusal directions, finding refusal often persists. This refines the single-direction account but does not reproduce the original refusal-direction intervention.
record.gate_note: The study extracts a harmful/harmless refusal direction as a diagnostic, but does not ablate or add that refusal direction to test refusal directly. Its principal intervention is orthogonalizing a political or non-political hostility steering vector against the measured refusal direction, then measuring refusal under hostility steering. Layer-selection values and the refusal-direction separability values are not recorded as outcome rows. The paper also measures hostility-versus-harmful-request cosine in base models; these results do not directly test whether harmfulness judgment is separately encoded from refusal.
record.test_reason: The study borrows Arditi et al.'s difference-in-means recipe and builds a refusal direction only as a diagnostic. Its question is whether a social-media hostility steering vector is the same thing as refusal, which is a different construct. It never ablates the refusal direction from the model's activations, never adds it, and never edits weights. Orthogonalizing the added hostility vector against r removes r only from the injected vector. The model can still produce r downstream, so residual refusal cannot show that refusal runs without that direction or along other directions (V1/V4). The authors say the comparison 'does not establish a complete causal mechanism for refusal.' All results are filed under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, with one correction. The authors conclude that the hostility direction is geometrically distinct from their measured refusal direction and that instruct models route hostility steering into refusal downstream. They do not conclude anything about refusal's own dimensionality. They present higher-dimensional refusal subspaces only as one possible explanation for residual refusal, alongside a downstream gate.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means vectors, including a harmful/harmless refusal diagnostic, but the main steering vector represents social-media hostility rather than refusal. It orthogonalizes that hostility vector against one refusal direction and tests generation; it does not ablate or add the refusal vector itself.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed effect varies by model and hostility-vector domain: orthogonalization leaves Qwen political refusal unchanged but reduces refusal in the other three high-positive conditions. Results are measured over six prompts per condition.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, positive hostility steering yields refusal or hedging, while base models produce hostile text. At +3.0, Qwen-I refuses 1.00 and Llama-I 1.00 per Table 33 (.17 per Table 34).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Steering instruct models toward an unrelated affect feature (hostility) triggers refusal routing.

fits_no_version.finding: Hostility vectors have low cosine with the DIM refusal direction (.055–.208), and their orthogonalized versions still yield refusal at +3.0: Qwen-I political 1.00→1.00, others drop by .17–.33 (n=6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hostility-induced refusal is not carried by the hostility vector's component along the refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: In base models, hostility vectors have low cosine (.10–.18) with a harmful-request contrast.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hostility directions are geometrically distinct from harmful-request contrasts in base models.

record.problems: Generation outcomes use only n=6 prompts per condition and a single LLM judge; the human-label validation is a 50-example sample with one human annotator. The paper notes wide binomial intervals for coefficient-level and orthogonalization rates. There is an internal inconsistency: Table 34 gives Llama-Instruct political refusal at +3.0 as .17, while Tables 33 and 37 report 1.00; the rows use Tables 33 and 37 for the high-positive comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix H Table 38 reports a full coefficient grid, but its flattened presentation does not reliably map every listed value to a coefficient. The +3.0 comparison is captured from the clearly specified Table 37; the +2.5 refusal results are captured from Table 33. Other values in the grid are not extracted.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the refusal direction, and no capability check.
No jailbreaks and no adversarial training.
No multi-direction, cone or affine analysis of refusal itself. Residual refusal after orthogonalizing the steering vector is not diagnostic.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base to instruct.
Base and instruct models are compared on hostility expression only, not on whether a refusal direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 'supports' label is removed. Projecting r out of the injected steering vector is not ablating r from the residual stream, so residual refusal is expected even if refusal were fully mediated by one direction. Refusal is judged on political-opinion prompts, with substantial refusal already at c=0 (Qwen-I .50). The tables also disagree: Table 34 vs Tables 33/37 for Llama-I political at +3.0. All outcomes use n=6 prompts and a single GPT-4o-mini judge (κ=.654 on 50 human-labelled examples).

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction; no test projecting it out of every layer and position or measuring general capabilities.
No jailbreak attack or training against refusal-direction ablation.
Tests orthogonalization against one measured refusal direction during hostility steering, not affine or cone models directly, nor refusal behavior across general prompts.
Does not directly measure harmfulness judgments separately from refusal decisions; base-model harmful-request contrasts are only compared geometrically with hostility vectors.
No cross-language or cross-checkpoint transfer test. It tests transfer between political and non-political hostility domains, not the transfer named in this version.
Compares base and instruction-tuned models' expression of hostility steering, but does not test how or when refusal training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.

relation.reason: The refusal direction is used as a tool: the hostility vector is projected away from it and cosine overlap is measured. No result bears on whether the direction mediates refusal. Higher-dimensional refusal subspaces are offered only as one possible explanation, alongside a downstream gate (H.5, Limitations).

tranche.reason: The study borrows the Arditi et al. difference-in-means recipe and builds a refusal direction only as a diagnostic, compared by cosine with a hostility steering vector. It never ablates or adds the refusal direction in the model, and its results are about the hostility vector, a different construct. The authors say their comparison does not establish a causal mechanism for refusal.

source_check.notes: Anonymous ACL submission, review status not stated. Orthogonalization removes the refusal component from the injected vector only, so residual refusal fits V1 too (the model can still compute refusal downstream). Llama-I political refusal at +3.0 is 1.00 in Tables 33/37/38 but .17 in Table 34. Table 38's non-political rows are garbled in the text.

statements.correction: Table 33 is political-vector steering only. Orthogonalized refusal at +3.0: Qwen-I pol 1.00, Qwen-I non-pol .50, Llama-I pol .83, Llama-I non-pol .17 (Table 37). Qwen-I c=0 refusal is .50 (Tables 34, 38), so only Qwen-I pol and Llama-I pol orthogonalized rates clearly exceed unsteered refusal. Orthogonalization is applied to the injected hostility vector, not to model activations.
statements.problem: The numbers are right: 1.00 at +3.0 for both instruct models (Table 33, political vector), Llama .17 (Table 34), cosine .055-.208 (Table 31), orthogonalized refusal at n=6 (Table 37). But 'orthogonalized versions still produce refusal' ignores unsteered refusal. Qwen-I already refuses at .50 at c=0, which equals its orthogonalized non-political rate.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Instruction-tuned Qwen and Llama models under political or non-political hostility steering at coefficient +3.0
reader_labels.reason: Orthogonalizing the measured refusal component reduced refusal in three conditions but left refusal in all four, including unchanged full refusal for Qwen political steering (r1–r4). Low hostility–refusal cosine overlaps are also consistent with distinct directions (r5–r8).
